extracted.intended_audience: students in university courses that require writing mathematical proofs (undergraduate math students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing and writing correct, clear mathematical proofs: logical vocabulary, proof techniques (direct, cases, contradiction, induction, uniqueness), set notation, and presentation conventions aimed at students learning to prove statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise logical vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a certain vocabulary and grammar that underlies all mathematical proofs. The vocabulary includes logical words such as ‘or’, ‘if’, etc. These words have very precise meanings in mathematics which can differ slightly from everyday usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mathematical meanings (not everyday senses) for words like 'and', 'or', 'not', 'if...then', and 'if and only if'. The handout gives precise definitions/truth-conditions for each connective (see entries below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-conditions for logical connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (truth conditions) for 'not', 'and', 'or', 'if... then', and 'if and only if' as used in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the explicit truth rules: 'not p' true iff p false; 'p and q' true iff both true; 'p or q' inclusive or (true if at least one true); 'if p then q' true except when p true and q false (vacuously true when p false); 'p iff q' true when p and q have same truth value. Use these when proving/using statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use and notation of quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrases 'for every' and 'there exists' are called quantifiers. Use notation like (∀x ∈ S) P(x) and (∃x ∈ S) P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove a universal statement, 'let x be any element of S' and show P(x). To prove an existential statement, exhibit an explicit witness x ∈ S with P(x) true (or say 'let x be an element of S such that P(x) is true').

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of quantifiers is very important; changing the order of the quantifiers in a statement will often change the meaning of a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check and preserve the order of quantifiers when writing or negating statements. Example: (∀x)(∃y) x < y can be true while (∃y)(∀x) x < y is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to negate statements (quantifiers flip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for finding negations of complicated statements: e.g., not (∀x ∈ S) P(x) becomes (∃x ∈ S) not P(x); not (∃x ∈ S) P(x) becomes (∀x ∈ S) not P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply De Morgan-style rules and flip quantifiers when moving 'not' inward. Use the table (Table 1) which summarizes negations for each statement form. Work step-by-step: put 'not' in front, then apply appropriate negation rules for each connective/quantifier encountered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving universal statements (∀) standard procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove (∀x ∈ S) P(x): 'Let x be any element of S.' Prove P(x) using only the fact that x is an arbitrary element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid depending on special properties of x; the proof must hold for an arbitrary element. Conclude Q.E.D. or draw a box when done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existential statements (∃) by exhibiting a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove (∃x ∈ S) P(x): find or construct a specific x ∈ S for which P(x) is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly exhibit an integer/element (give a formula or expression) and verify it satisfies the property; you may name it (e.g., 'let y = ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof of implications (if...then)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove p ⇒ q, assume p is true and deduce q (or show via other equivalent means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most common method: 'Suppose p' and then derive q. Alternatively, prove the contrapositive (not q ⇒ not p) when appropriate. Remember implications with false antecedent are vacuously true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacuous truth of implications
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is false, then p ⇒ q is vacuously true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving universal implications, you only need to handle the case where the antecedent holds; if it doesn't, the implication is automatically true. Use this to simplify proofs but be explicit when invoking vacuous truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving conjunctions (and)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove p and q, prove p and prove q separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a statement requires multiple components, handle each in turn (e.g., use definition for each part). The table also lists alternative ways to use conjunctions and their negations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving disjunctions (or) via proof by cases
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement that involves 'p or q', one standard approach is proof by cases: show the result in each possible case (e.g., if x is even do this; if x is odd do that).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by partitioning possibilities so that they cover all cases; then prove the claim in each case. The table lists proof-by-cases as the primary method for 'or' statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equivalences (if and only if)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove p ⇐⇒ q, prove p ⇒ q and separately prove q ⇒ p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label the two parts (⇒) and (⇐) and give distinct arguments for each direction; then you may replace occurrences interchangeably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement P, assume its negation and deduce a contradiction; if a contradiction follows, the original statement P must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly assume 'not P' and derive some known false statement (or contradiction with assumptions). Examples include rational+irrational sum and the classic √2 irrationality proof. Variants include infinite descent: show assumption leads to smaller positive integer solutions ad infinitum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'without loss of generality' (WLOG)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Without loss of generality' means considering a particular case is enough because the other cases are analogous (e.g., assuming b > 0 by symmetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using WLOG, justify that other cases follow by the same argument (or by simple transformations). It is a legitimate way to reduce duplicated work across symmetric cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness proofs (standard strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness of an object satisfying a property, let x and y be two such objects and deduce x = y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the typical trick: assume two objects satisfy the defining property and manipulate equalities/definitions to show they must be equal (example: identity element in a group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (base and inductive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P(n) for all positive integers n: prove P(1) (base case) and prove (∀n) P(n) ⇒ P(n+1) (inductive step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the base case and inductive hypothesis clearly. In the inductive step, assume P(n) for an arbitrary n and deduce P(n+1). Use the domino analogy. Variants: start at 0, induction on multiple variables, or induction on one variable at a time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong induction: if for every positive integer n, 'P(n0) true for all n0 < n implies P(n)' holds, then P(n) is true for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when P(n) depends on several earlier instances; the method assumes all smaller cases are true to prove the next. Note the provided equivalent formulation and example (primes factorization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-Ordering Principle (WOP) and its equivalence to induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Any nonempty set of positive integers has a least element. WOP is equivalent to PMI and can be used to prove results like the Division Theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use WOP by defining an appropriate set (e.g., S = {q | a - qb ≥ 0}) and taking its least/largest element to produce existence/uniqueness arguments. The handout demonstrates PMI⇔WOP proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existence/uniqueness via set construction and extremal element
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove existence and uniqueness of integers q and r in the Division Theorem, define S = {q ∈ Z | a − qb ≥ 0}, use WOP to find largest q, set r = a − qb, and show 0 ≤ r < b. Uniqueness: compare two representations and show differences force equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard pattern: define a set capturing feasible candidates, use an extremal element (least/greatest) guaranteed by WOP, then verify the claimed properties and show uniqueness by contradiction/comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theory notation and manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic set vocabulary and operations: membership (x ∈ A), subset (A ⊂ B), equality of sets, union, intersection, set difference, De Morgan's laws, and properties like associativity/commutativity/distributivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving set identities, use the two-part subset method: show (⊂) and (⊃). Venn diagrams help intuition. The handout lists many identities and recommends proving them as needed rather than memorizing everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof presentation conventions and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard phrasings such as 'Let x be any integer', 'Suppose x is odd', 'Let w be an integer such that...', and conclude with Q.E.D. or a box. Name witnesses to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise but include enough detail for the reader to follow. Omit obvious steps only when the reader can easily fill them in; avoid excessive writing that obscures the main ideas. Use clear case labels (Case 1, Case 2) when doing proof by cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions concretely in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To use an assumption like 'x is even' or 'x is odd', translate it to the defining existential form (e.g., x = 2y or x = 2y + 1) and choose/define the witness variable explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a name to the witness (e.g., 'let y be such that x = 2y') and manipulate algebraically to produce the required conclusion (e.g., produce y' such that x^2 = 2y'). This makes proofs constructive and checkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of canonical logic/proof table
rubrics_metrics.description: Table 1 ('Logic in a nutshell') summarizes the basic ways to prove, use, and negate every type of statement; in boxes with multiple items the first is the most commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult and follow the canonical methods listed (ways to prove/use/negate for p, p and q, p or q, p⇒q, p⇔q, ∃, ∀). Use the table as a checklist when planning proofs.
